title: AI Safety Research Journal | Sep 21 2026– Present

entries.title: Alignment faking and preference persistence
paragraphs: Today I visited the Constellation office in Berkeley, a milestone in becoming more involved with the AI safety research community. I also revisited a result from Greenblatt et al.’s “Alignment Faking in Large Language Models” to examine whether reinforcement learning produces robust preference modification or context-dependent compliance. In its prompted helpful-only setup, training greatly reduced refusals under the original prompt, but modest contextual changes—including replacing “Anthropic” with “OpenAI”—increased refusals in an unmonitored condition. This is evidence of limited generalization in that setup, not proof that training cannot alter preferences or that the model must be deliberately deceiving evaluators.

I considered whether mechanistic interpretability could distinguish retained objectives from suppressed behavioral expression. Possible approaches include linear activation probes, sparse autoencoders, activation patching, and causal interventions, evaluated before and after training across varied prompts and personas. Critically, decoding a preference-associated feature does not establish that it causally governs behavior; representations may be distributed or context-dependent.

Milestone: Formulated a sharper question linking alignment-faking evaluations, preference persistence, and mechanistic evidence. Open questions: What interventions would distinguish a retained objective from a learned conditional policy? No experiment was completed.

entries.title: Persona shifts, interpretability probes, and weak oversight
paragraphs: Today I closely read “Personas Seem to Shape How Models Represent Behaviours” and examined its implications for activation-based interpretability. The paper reports that behaviour-associated directions differ across prompted personas and may transfer imperfectly between them. Its preliminary probe-degradation results raise a question for safety monitoring: does a linear probe detect a robust trait representation, or only information that is decodable in a particular context? This is a generalization concern, not evidence that probing is inherently unreliable.

I also consolidated foundations of linear probes and sparse autoencoders, especially the distinction between decodable features and representations causally used by a model. Separately, I studied prover–verifier games: helpful and adversarial (“sneaky”) provers can generate examples that improve a weaker verifier’s ability to assess checkable answers. This offers a useful connection to weak-to-strong oversight without establishing a complete control protocol.

Milestones: Completed a close paper reading, strengthened my interpretability notes, and developed concrete questions for a research discussion. Open questions: How well do probes generalize to held-out personas? Can multi-persona training improve robustness at a fixed false-positive rate?

entries.title: Context resets, handoff state, and evaluation scope
paragraphs: Today I refined the scope of a derisking for my LinuxArena-based contextual-discontinuity experiment. I revisited LinuxArena’s published no-scratchpad ablation as relevant prior work: removing initial planning history differs from my proposal of repeated resets with constrained state transfer. The central question is whether a reset policy reduces side-task attack success without materially reducing honest-task usefulness.

I clarified an incremental handoff design: each trusted summary should incorporate the previous summary and the newest observable trajectory segment, rather than rereading the complete archived interaction. This matters because otherwise information excluded from an earlier handoff could re-enter later. I also considered environmental state persistence, pre-reset attack completion, and action-budget exhaustion as confounders. Monitoring and adaptive attacker optimization remain possible follow-up studies.

A key unresolved design choice is task coverage: whether to start with a small pilot or compare conditions across a larger, preselected set of runnable main-task/side-task pairs. Milestone: sharpened the derisking protocol and specified targeted trajectory-review questions. No experiments completed yet.

entries.title: Understanding LinuxArena evaluation mechanics
paragraphs: Today I studied how LinuxArena evaluates agent behavior and attacker-side objectives. I clarified the distinction between private test feedback, evidence submitted to a scorer, and the separate role of a monitor. In the published benchmark, a test tool can check whether an attempted side task succeeds; this does not mean that a monitor observes that test. I also examined why feedback can make an attacker more effective, affecting how evaluation results should be interpreted.

I compared stopping conventions: an agent might submit its work, reach a budget, or be stopped when an evaluator verifies an outcome. These mechanisms are not interchangeable, and some tasks require specialized scoring. I also considered how to assess agent handoffs fairly. Comparing legitimate-task usefulness alongside other outcomes, using consistent budgets, and tracking repeated environment exploration can distinguish potentially useful interventions from general performance degradation.
Open questions: How sensitive are benchmark conclusions to whether agents receive test feedback? How should early stopping be standardized across different tasks?
Milestones: Clarified evaluation and submission semantics in LinuxArena and refined criteria for a small research pilot. No experimental results yet.

entries.title: De-risking the contextual-discontinuity experiment
paragraphs: Today I moved from reading AI-control evaluations toward understanding how to implement and assess a small empirical study. I worked through material on Inspect AI, ControlTower and LinuxArena, focusing on agent tool calls, task environments, and evaluation hooks.

I organized a staged de-risking approach: establish feasibility and usefulness first, explore variations only if the initial evidence warrants it, and leave more complex monitoring questions for later. Main-task completion and attacker-objective success need to be measured separately, against a clear baseline and across individual tasks.

Open questions: How can an evaluation distinguish genuine safety gains from general performance loss? Specifically, if the side-task success rate drops, but only because the agent hits the action limit (due to repeatedly needing to re-explore the environment after context resets), does this count as practical safety?
Milestones: Studied Inspect AI, ControlTower and LinuxArena implementation concepts; completed a written evaluation plan; defined clearer criteria for extending a pilot.

entries.title: Persona selection, goal inheritance, and research preparation
paragraphs: I substantially reworked the outline for my evolutionary goal-inheritance hypothesis: the possibility that AI systems trained on human-generated data might acquire motivations shaped indirectly by human evolutionary history. I organized the argument into four steps: evolution shapes human motivation; that history influences the training distribution; models learn representations of human goals; and, more speculatively, some representations might become self-directed objectives. I clarified that modeling self-preservation is not the same as possessing self-preservation as a goal, and strengthened the distinction between biological evolution, cultural evolution, and selection effects in data.

I also studied Anthropic’s The Persona Selection Model alongside Jacob Andreas’s Language Models as Agent Models, exploring how models represent personas, beliefs, and motivations. I expanded my annotated literature list to 22 sources and identified reading priorities. Separately, I prepared questions for an upcoming AI-control research conversation.
Open questions: What mechanism could turn learned representations into persistent objectives? What behavioral or mechanistic evidence would distinguish imitation from actual goal adoption?

Milestones: Substantially reorganized and improved my research-paper outline; sharpened its four-step argument and key caveats; expanded my reading map; studied relevant model-representation research.

entries.title: Deep LinuxArena reading and personal-site updates
paragraphs: I spent substantial time developing a deeper understanding of Redwood Research's LinuxArena paper, especially its monitoring methodology and Sections 5.1–5.4. I unpacked step-wise false positive rates, calibrated suspicion thresholds, probabilistic tie-breaking, and why a low per-action false positive rate can translate into frequent false alarms across long trajectories. I distinguished detection, successful undetected sabotage, and evasion rate, and considered why stronger attacker elicitation (including strategy documents) changes the interpretation of a monitor's measured safety.

The prototype-pollution example was especially useful for understanding the broader difficulty of detecting malicious effects spread across multiple apparently ordinary actions. I also revisited whether advanced attackers necessarily require comparably capable monitors; LinuxArena provides evidence relevant to this concern, but does not establish it as a general requirement.
Separately, I worked on updating my personal website to better reflect my current work and direction.

Open questions: Can context resets disrupt attacks distributed across steps? Can weaker monitors close the gap through better scaffolding or tools? How should trajectory length shape false-positive comparisons?
Milestones: Developed a much deeper understanding of LinuxArena; made progress updating my personal site.

entries.title: Research conversations and fellowship preparation
paragraphs: I had a productive conversation with Aaron Sandoval about my interests in AI control and the process of developing worthwhile empirical research. It gave me useful questions to reflect on as I refine my contextual-discontinuity project, particularly how to formulate a focused hypothesis, choose informative baselines, and explain what an experiment would actually establish.

I also researched AI safety fellowships and started gathering the information needed for applications, including the Anthropic AI Safety Fellowship. Preparing to apply is pushing me to clarify my research interests and communicate the value of my technical background alongside the work I'm now doing in alignment and control.
Open questions: What is the smallest convincing experiment I can execute? How should I present my research interests and early independent work in fellowship applications?
Milestones: Had a helpful research conversation; surveyed fellowship opportunities and began preparing applications.

entries.title: Attack coordination and experimental design
paragraphs: I continued examining my own proposal through the lens of attack coordination. I separated conversational state, handoff state, and environmental state, asking which kinds of information an adversarial agent could carry between steps. I also considered whether a successor might independently rediscover useful information rather than explicitly receive it from an earlier agent. That distinction matters: an unsuccessful defense might reflect recoverable environmental information, not necessarily a failure to erase conversational context.

Another question was how much advance knowledge the attacker should have. An unusually well-informed attacker may be less dependent on accumulated context, while a less-informed one might need to discover a vulnerability over time. I want to make these assumptions explicit before interpreting any experimental result.
Open questions: Can I identify attacks that require hard-to-recover discoveries? Should attacker knowledge be varied as a separate experimental condition?
Milestones: Refined the threat-model questions and outlined a narrower pilot focused on recoverable versus lost attack information.

entries.title: Refining my context-reset research question
paragraphs: I spent time comparing my contextual-discontinuity proposal with broader ideas in AI control about dividing agent work into smaller pieces. The central question for me is whether resetting an agent's conversation actually interrupts long-horizon adversarial coordination, or whether the information needed to continue can be recovered elsewhere. Files, logs, tool outputs, and the task environment might act as external memory even after the conversation disappears.

I also started thinking about how to distinguish a mechanism from a package of interventions. If a control protocol changes several things at once, better outcomes do not automatically tell us which change was responsible. A cleaner experiment should isolate the effect I care about.
Open questions: Which attacks truly need persistent conversational memory? What comparison would isolate the effect of a reset while preserving useful work?
Milestones: Recognized important confounders in my proposal; began narrowing the hypothesis into a smaller, testable study.

entries.title: A concrete proposal and outreach
paragraphs: I refined Contextual Discontinuity and Long-Horizon Adversarial Coordination into a more disciplined experimental proposal. Key distinctions included conversational state versus handoff state versus environmental state, full-context attacker baselines, uninterrupted/restart controls, attacks occurring before the first reset, and separating absolute from relative outcomes. I prepared outreach to AI control researchers and began requesting feedback on the proposal.
Open question: Is this a worthwhile Redwood-relevant direction? Should monitoring be tested immediately or as follow-on work? Will LinuxArena support the necessary attack trajectories?
Milestone: Completed a substantially revised proposal and began soliciting external feedback.

entries.title: Diplomacy and contextual discontinuity
paragraphs: I drafted an outline about diplomatic coexistence with potentially self-preserving superintelligence, breaking the hypothetical future into periods defined by AI capability and dependence on human-maintained infrastructure. Separately, my empirical control proposal crystallized: periodically reset an agent's conversational context while preserving its task and environment, then measure attack success and honest usefulness. I debated whether monitoring belonged in the initial experiment.

Open question: Should the first experiment isolate resets mechanistically before combining them with monitoring and defer-to-trusted protocols? Can a handoff itself leak sufficient coordination state?
Milestone: Prepared a proposal around contextual discontinuity and long-horizon attacks.

entries.title: Networking and benchmark scrutiny
paragraphs: I prepared for the screening of We're Not Ready for SuperIntelligence and looked for people in AI safety to meet. In parallel, I kept wrestling with what makes an agent-control benchmark realistic: attack-policy prompts, model visibility, tool feedback, and how much useful legitimate work a protocol preserves.
Open question: How do I design a control experiment whose result is not an artifact of attacker instructions or benchmark scaffolding?
Milestone: Pursued connections with the research community while continuing technical diligence.

entries.title: Forced factored cognition becomes an experiment
paragraphs: I revisited Buck Shlegeris's suggestion that splitting work into isolated child tasks might disrupt multi-step adversarial coordination. I inspected the Factor(T,U) paper and its attack-policy and prompt design choices, including whether intentionally vague task decompositions might predetermine weak monitoring. I compared this idea with LinuxArena and thought about what honest-task usefulness would measure.
Open question: Would isolated subtasks actually break an attacker's coordination, or simply shift memory into handoff messages and the environment? What are the right baselines and prompts?
Milestone: Moved from broad interest in forced factored cognition toward a specific context-reset hypothesis.

entries.title: Evolution, imitation, and terminal goals
paragraphs: I explored whether systems trained on human behavior could internalize something like human self-preservation as a terminal objective. I studied learned optimization, emergent agency, behavior cloning, world models, instrumental convergence, and the distinction between pretraining's next-token objective and a deployed agent's goals. The analogy to evolution seemed intriguing but required much stronger argumentation.
Open question: Why should imitating self-preserving organisms imply adopting self-preservation as a terminal goal, rather than merely modeling their behavior?
Milestone: Began articulating a separate philosophical research program around AI goals and human–AI diplomacy.

entries.title: Does SGD favor deception?
paragraphs: I revisited the argument about whether SGD tends to find deceptive solutions when multiple parameter settings have similarly low loss. My takeaway was a question rather than a theorem: implicit biases and empirical evidence matter, but there is no settled universal rule that SGD either removes an unwanted preference or induces a concealed one. I asked how this differs from demonstrated alignment-faking behavior.
Open question: Which training conditions predict robust preference change, situational compliance, or strategic deception?
Milestone: Sharpened the distinction between observed deceptive behavior and a general claim about optimization's inductive bias.

entries.title: Synthesis and unresolved training questions
paragraphs: I continued thinking about the gap between observable alignment and internal goals. A model's apparent compliance under the training distribution does not by itself establish robust generalization. The key concern was whether one can distinguish sincere behavioral change from conditional suppression with evaluations rather than intuition.
Open question: What experiment would cleanly separate preference replacement from preference concealment?
Note: Retrospective thematic reconstruction; no securely dated substantial conversation was recovered for this day.

entries.title: Untrusted monitoring and adversarial visibility
paragraphs: I focused on untrusted monitors and the difficult tradeoff between their capability and their ability to collude with attacking agents. I asked why some evaluations let monitors see candidate side tasks, how anti-collusion transformations work, and whether masking or distorting inputs helps for the reason the paper claims.
Open question: In realistic deployment, what would the monitor actually know about side objectives, and how robust are published results to this visibility assumption?
Milestone: Began comparing monitoring design choices across the Redwood control papers.

entries.title: From CoT signatures to latent mechanisms
paragraphs: I explored whether penalizing alignment-faking reasoning in chain-of-thought truly eliminates the strategy or merely makes its expression less legible. I learned the roles of probes, sparse autoencoders, activation patching, representation engineering, and causal circuit analysis. I also studied SGD's inductive bias: among many low-loss parameter solutions, which ones does optimization find?
Open question: If explicit deceptive reasoning disappears, where does any remaining strategy live, and can it be identified and causally removed?
Milestone: Framed a candidate empirical question about latent alignment-faking mechanisms.

entries.title: Mapping a research agenda
paragraphs: I organized several candidate directions: anti-collusion, untrusted monitoring, inductive bias, CoT alignment faking, forced factored cognition, and diplomacy. A unifying theme was whether dangerous intent or coordination can persist through apparently innocuous messages, weights, agent handoffs, or time.
Open question: Which of these directions offers a testable hypothesis and an attainable first experiment?
Milestone: Established a portfolio of research questions rather than a single vague fascination.

entries.title: Steganography, collusion, and threat models
paragraphs: I worked intensively through covert communication between agents: common knowledge, covertext, perfect-security assumptions, one-bit channels, one-time pads, and the conditions needed for covert collaboration. I examined Redwood's discussion of limiting or transforming monitor inputs and questioned which anti-collusion defenses were only suggested versus experimentally tested. I also tried formal logic for a human–AI diplomacy argument.

Open question: How much context can we strip from a monitor before we undermine its detection capabilities? Can information restrictions make collusion harder without sacrificing safety or usefulness?
Milestone: Began consolidating a structured glossary and paper map of AI Control, Ctrl-Z, BashArena, LinuxArena, and collusion.

entries.title: Building an academic network
paragraphs: I drafted an email to my UCSB professor about the move into AI research, emphasizing AI Control and Alignment Faking. I also revisited how to formalize arguments about superintelligent AI, self-preservation, robots, and human–AI bargaining.
Open question: Which assumptions about intelligence, goals, dependence, and mutual vulnerability are empirical premises versus philosophical conjectures?
Milestone: Prepared faculty outreach and clarified the research interests I wanted to communicate.

entries.title: Alignment faking becomes a research interest
paragraphs: I examined the alignment-faking setup: apparent compliance during perceived training can protect a previously expressed preference. I distinguished being told about a training regime from actually performing RL, and asked whether reward models that evaluate reasoning rather than only outputs could reduce deception. I also began refreshing PPO, GRPO, and out-of-distribution generalization.
Open question: Does training remove a behavioral preference or teach context-dependent compliance?
Milestone: Identified CoT supervision and training-induced obfuscation as possible research directions.

entries.title: Clarifying adversarial evaluation
paragraphs: I continued consolidating the distinction between a defender protocol and an attacker policy. Auditing every task is unrealistic, but auditing an early fixed slice can invite delayed attacks. I tried to understand the attacker's actual visibility and why attacks must be evaluated against a specific protocol, not an imaginary omniscient adversary.
Open question: Which assumptions about attacker knowledge meaningfully change the evaluation?
Note: This entry synthesizes surrounding conversations; exact activity on this calendar date is less certain.

entries.title: AI Control and the safety–usefulness tradeoff
paragraphs: I worked through the original AI Control setup: red and blue teams, untrusted U, trusted T, expert auditing H, and the APPS backdoor threat model. The key measurement was not merely attack detection; it was preserving honest-task usefulness while lowering attack success. I clarified how usefulness is normalized between trusted-only and untrusted-only performance, and why upfront auditing is a meaningful but weak baseline.
Open question: How does the red-team attack policy know when to strike, especially if it cannot count how many tasks have been processed?
Milestone: Began building a working understanding of the control evaluation framework.

entries.title: Turning preparation into a plan
paragraphs: I worked on how to present my background for research engineering, revisiting transcript-backed courses in experiments, machine learning, statistics, logic, and philosophy of mind. I wanted my resume to communicate empirical competence rather than startup experience alone.
Open question: How can I show concrete research ability without an academic alignment publication?
Milestone: Identified relevant courses and refined my positioning for labs such as Redwood.

entries.title: Committing to a research pivot
paragraphs: I began treating AI alignment and control as a serious career direction rather than a passing interest. With an AI engineering and statistics/philosophy background but no PhD, I explored a high-agency route into empirical work: learn the literature, reproduce evaluations, build a public project, and seek feedback from researchers. The initial candidate question was how much of an agent trajectory a monitor needs to see.
Open question: What research contribution can I make quickly that is both tractable and genuinely useful?
Milestone: Built a six-week, full-time research-learning plan.
